speaker: Elena Verna
title: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
question: In product growth, why does copying a successful competitor's onboarding or pricing flow usually fail to produce the same results?
guest: Knowing what your competition is doing is important, and being inspired by elements of their experience is a great input into ideation so you don't start from a blank page. But blatantly ripping their onboarding or pricing flows because they are successful fails 95 percent of the time. Every experience is unique to their specific customer and channel. Worse, you don't even know if you're seeing their actual winning control, an active test cell, or a personalized flow based on where you signed up from. At Dropbox, someone once reached out saying they loved one of our activation pages and were going to copy it—and we hadn't touched that page in ten years, it was only visible to a small cohort, and it performed terribly. You can spot recurring patterns across competitors as an ideation input, but you can never skip your own design cycle, user research, customer interviews, and experimentation.

points.core: Product flows are tightly coupled to each competitor's specific user context.
points.note: Accept: onboarding or pricing flows depend on the competitor's specific audience, customer segment, product, or acquisition channel, so they do not transfer directly. Do not credit: generic brand-voice or differentiation platitudes without user/channel fit.

points.core: Outsiders cannot tell whether a competitor's live page is a winning experience.
points.note: Accept: external observers cannot distinguish a winning control from an active A/B test cell, a personalized cohort flow, or an unmaintained low-performing legacy page. Do not credit: vague claims that competitors might not know what they are doing without the observability mechanism.

points.core: Copying skips the user validation needed to prove the flow fits your product.
points.note: Accept: competitor teardowns only serve as ideation inputs to avoid starting from scratch and cannot replace your own design cycle, user research, customer interviews, or experimentation. Do not credit: saying never look at competitors or merely saying customize the colors.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Copying a competitor's flow usually fails because you are copying the visible output of a process, not the conditions that made it work.

A competitor's onboarding or pricing was tuned to their context: their audience and its intent, their traffic sources, brand trust, product value and how quickly users reach it, their cost structure, and their competitive position. A well-known brand can ask for a credit card upfront or run a long signup questionnaire because users arrive already convinced; an unknown product using the same flow simply loses people. Pricing likewise reflects their customers' willingness to pay and their unit economics, not yours.

You also can't see what you're copying. The flow you observe may be an A/B test variant, a legacy design they haven't fixed, or something that succeeds despite itself. You see the surface, not the data, the failed experiments, or the supporting systems behind it, such as lifecycle emails, sales assist, and the product quality that drives retention.

Finally, a flow optimises for their goals and constraints, which may differ from yours. Competitor flows are best treated as hypotheses to test against your own users, not answers.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Copying a competitor's onboarding or pricing flow usually fails because you are replicating visible surface mechanics without the underlying growth system that makes them work. Effective activation and monetization depend on tight alignment among product value, audience intent, acquisition channel, and brand trust. Users arriving via high-intent word-of-mouth will tolerate friction—like upfront credit card gates or lengthy setup surveys—that immediately bounces cold paid-search traffic. Similarly, an incumbent's pricing reflects accumulated brand equity, mature switching costs, and established willingness to pay that a challenger rarely shares; copying their tiers or value metrics often stalls early adoption or obscures your product's distinct "aha" moment. Furthermore, outsiders face severe observability blind spots: you cannot tell whether a competitor succeeds *because* of a specific flow or *despite* it, nor can you see the backend sales-assist motions, lifecycle messaging, and retention loops supporting that experience. Because growth levers are highly sensitive to company stage and user psychology, transplanting another product's mature solutions onto your unique friction points almost always underperforms.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Copying a competitor's onboarding or pricing usually fails because you see the visible surface of their system but not the conditions that make it work. A flow is fitted to its context. That includes the company's users and their intent, its acquisition channels, the product's "aha moment," its brand trust, network effects, sales motion and unit economics. Slack's onboarding works because teammates are already waiting inside. Notion's freemium tier works because templates and word-of-mouth bring in users who have already decided to try it. Put the same screens in front of different users who arrive with different expectations and they behave differently.

There's also survivorship and timing bias. You're copying the version that exists today, not the hundreds of experiments behind it, and you don't know which elements actually drive results and which are leftover or even hurting them. Their flow may also be tuned for goals you don't share, such as enterprise upsell or data collection.

Finally, copying skips the learning. The competitor's advantage is the insight about their customers that produced the flow, not the flow itself. A better approach is to treat competitors' designs as ideas to test and validate them against your own users' jobs-to-be-done, activation data and willingness to pay.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Copying a competitor’s onboarding or pricing flow usually fails because those flows are only the visible surface of a much deeper system. What converts for a competitor depends heavily on their specific audience, acquisition channels, brand trust, and user intent. A paywall or multi-step setup that works for a well-known leader with high-intent traffic will often cause steep drop-offs for a challenger still earning credibility.

Equally important, effective onboarding and pricing are tightly coupled to how a particular product delivers its core value. A competitor’s pricing tiers reflect their unique value metric, cost structure, and retention dynamics, while their onboarding is tuned to their specific time-to-value and activation moment. Transplanting those mechanics onto a different product creates friction rather than clarity. Finally, outsiders only see a static snapshot—never the experiments, trade-offs, or downstream churn behind it, nor whether that flow is even working well for the competitor in the first place.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An onboarding or pricing flow works because it fits the customers and product around it. A competitor’s users may arrive with more trust, clearer intent, or a different willingness to pay. Its onboarding might skip steps because users already understand the product, while your users need those steps to reach their first useful outcome.

You can see the competitor’s screens, but you rarely see its traffic mix, experiment results, or trade-offs. A pricing change that lifts trial sign-ups might also reduce paid conversions or retention. Use the competitor’s flow to form a hypothesis about what helps users, then test that idea with your own audience and measure the outcome you actually want.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A competitor’s onboarding or pricing flow is only one part of what drives conversion. Their users may arrive ready to buy, already trust the brand, or understand the product’s value. Your users may still be deciding whether it solves their problem. The same prompt to choose a paid plan can feel like a convenient next step to one group and a reason to leave to the other.

You can see the flow, but you usually can’t see how those users would have behaved without it. The competitor may succeed partly because of that design or despite it. Treat the flow as a hypothesis. Identify the user problem you think it solves, check whether your users face it, and test whether the change improves the outcome you care about.
